title: Eight thoughts of a great person
hookLine: alone in a bamboo grove, Anuruddha thinks seven thoughts about what the teaching is for; the Buddha comes, praises him, and adds the eighth (AN 8.30)

cards: The boy who never heard no is now a monk, sitting by himself in a bamboo grove in the country of the Cetis. Nobody is teaching him. He's working something out, and the Anguttara Nikaya records it line by line.
This teaching, he thinks, is for one who wants little, not one who wants much. For one who is content, not discontent. He keeps going, one pair at a time, until he has seven.
Then, the text says, the Buddha knows his thought and appears in front of him, as quickly as a strong man stretches out his arm.

teach.h: SEVEN THOUGHTS, EACH WITH ITS OPPOSITE.
teach.b: First, the seven. The teaching is for one with few wants, not many. Content, not discontent.
Secluded, not fond of company. Energetic, not lazy.
With mindfulness set up, not muddled. Collected, not scattered. Wise, not foolish.
Each one names its opposite, so you can tell which way you're facing. Second, the praise and the gift. Good, good, Anuruddha, the Buddha says.

You have thought the thoughts of a great person. Then he adds one more: this teaching is for one who delights in non-proliferation, the mind that doesn't spin one thought into a hundred. Eight thoughts of a great person.
Third, few wants you can touch.

teach.h: A RAG ROBE LIKE A CHEST OF CLOTHES.
teach.b: For one who lives by these eight, the Buddha says, a rag robe seems like a householder's chest of colorful clothes. A lump of alms food, like fine rice. The foot of a tree, like a house with a peaked roof.
Plain medicine, like butter and honey. Few wants isn't a punishment here; it's a way of seeing plain things as enough. Fourth, what happened next.
Anuruddha stays in that grove, living by what he'd been told, and the text says he reached the goal.
The seven thoughts were his own. The eighth was a gift. And the first of them is today's line.
From the boy who had never heard there isn't, that's quite a road.

how: The eight thoughts of a great person (mahapurisavitakka) are taught in Theravada communities as a short list for reflection, and some monastics and lay meditators recite or review them as a check on their practice.

games.q: Anuruddha's eight thoughts: tap the pairs.
p: like a chest of colorful clothes

s: the Buddha gave Anuruddha all eight thoughts in a talk
Anuruddha thought seven on his own; the Buddha praised him and added the eighth.
few wants, not many; content, not discontent; and so on through the list.
few wants is taught as a punishment
the text says plain things come to seem like riches: a rag robe like a chest of clothes, the foot of a tree like a house.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a student, alone in a grove, has worked out seven true thoughts by himself. what do you do?
o: leave him alone; he's doing fine.
praise him, and add one more.
correct the list and start over.
games.why: "good, good, Anuruddha", and then the eighth: the teaching is for one who delights in not spinning, not in spinning.

practice: Pick just one of the eight.

Few wants: let the next small want that rises, a snack, a scroll, a sound, pass without feeding it; contentment: let one plain thing, a chair, a cup, be enough for a minute; or not spinning: when a thought starts to multiply, come back to one breath.
Whichever you choose, hold it lightly, the way Anuruddha held his, alone in the grove.

wordCard.voice: Appiccha, having few wants. The first of Anuruddha's seven thoughts in the bamboo grove, with the Buddha's eighth added: not spinning. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali appiccha: having few wants. The first of Anuruddha's thoughts.

carryVoice: Your line: few wants. Plain things, seen clearly, can be enough. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.30 (Anuruddha: the eight thoughts of a great person)
